list.listitem: While many organizations recommend screening asymptomatic pregnant women for iron deficiency anemia, the USPSTF reports insufficient evidence.B
High-risk infants in the age groups 6 to 12 months should receive iron supplementation, but the efficacy of screening all infants in this age group is uncertain.B
Ferritin is the best test to diagnose iron deficiency anemia.C
Patients older than 65 years with iron deficiency anemia should be screened for gastrointestinal malignancy.C
Treatment is with 60 to 65 mg of elemental iron taken orally in a fasting state as ferrous sulfate or ferrous gluconate.B

background.definition: Iron deficiency anemia (IDA) is characterized by diminished red blood cell production resulting from low levels of iron stored in the body.

list.listitem: The global prevalence of iron deficiency anemia varies greatly by country and region, but it is estimated to be around 20%
Most common nutritional disorder worldwide
Associated with adverse cognitive and behavioral test scores in children
Inadequate dietary intake of iron
Decreased absorption: malabsorption from disease such as celiac disease, postgastrectomy, or with acute or chronic inflammation
Increased iron loss: menstrual bleeding, acute or chronic gastrointestinal causes or hemolysis, blood donation, or phlebotomy
Increased demand: rapid growth in infancy or adolescence, pregnancy, or erythropoietin in malignancy

Erythropoiesis: iron stores are depleted in this stage, leading to a decrease in serum iron and increase in total iron binding capacity. Hemoglobin synthesis is unaffected initially, but, when transferrin is <15% to 20%, hemoglobin synthesis is reduced.

With IDA, there is appearance of microcytic red blood cells, and the hemoglobin and hematocrit begin to decrease. In moderate iron deficiency with hemoglobin in the range of 9-11 g/dL, the bone marrow is hypoproliferative. In severe anemia with hemoglobin 7 to 8 g/dL, there is prominent hypochromia with microcytosis and poikilocytes, and target cells start to appear. Consequently, with severe prolonged anemia, erythroid hyperplasia develops.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Native American or Alaskan Helicobacter pylori

list.listitem: Pregnant women are traditionally screened for IDA at the first prenatal visit although there is insufficient evidence to support this practice. USPSTF stated that the current evidence is insufficient to recommend routine iron supplementation in non-anemia pregnant women due to inadequate evidence on maternal health or birth outcomes.B A Cochrane review has shown that prenatal supplementation with iron or iron+folic acid (provided either daily or weekly) prevents anemia and iron deficiency at term.A The same Cochrane review has shown possible benefits of preventive iron supplementation in pregnant women as compared to controls on low birth weight (RR 0.84, 95% CI 0.69-1.03, low quality evidence) and preterm babies (RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.84-1.03, moderate quality evidence).B Maternal anemia is associated with preterm birth and low birth weight.

A Cochrane review has shown daily iron supplementation may reduce the prevalence of iron deficient anemia in menstruating women at the expense of gastrointestinal side effects .Recommendations for preventive iron supplementation in developed countries likely need revision.
The AAFP and AAP recommend screening for IDA routinely in asymptomatic children aged 6 months to 1 year. However, the USPSTF found insufficient evidence to support this approach.B
The USPSTF found a gap in the evidence that assess the effect of iron supplementation for iron deficiency anemia on growth or cognitive or neuro developmental outcomes in children aged 6-24 months.B

Routine screening for iron deficiency anemia is recommended for patients with heart failure by 2013 ACCF/AHA and 2016 European Society of Cardiology guidelines.B Routine screening of other populations is not addressed by guidelines.C
In adult blood donors, low dose iron supplementation reduces time to recovery of hemoglobin values after donation.
Hemoglobin and serum ferritin are the best tests to diagnose IDA.C
Patients older than 65 years with IDA have an increased risk of gastrointestinal malignancy.C

The American Gastroenterological Association (AGA) recommends screening asymptomatic post-menopausal women and men with IDA for gastrointestinal malignancies with both esophagogastroduodenoscopy and colonoscopy. C

Diagnosis.Diagnostic_criteria:
CDC criteria for anemia by hemoglobin value:
Infants <5 years old: <11 g/dL Children 5-12 years old: <11.5 g/dL Non-pregnant women: <12 g/dL Pregnant women, first trimester: <11 g/dL Pregnant women, second trimester: <10.5 g/dL Men: <13.5 g/dL

list.listitem: Patients with IDA are often asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic. Suspect anemia in patients with pallor or fatigue. Other symptoms include dyspnea, chest pain, and orthostasis.
Presence of conjunctiva pallor is moderately accurate for diagnosis of any anemia. Pallor may also exist at other sites (palms, gums, nail beds, skin).
In a study of 1,104 children under the age of 5 years in Malawi, pallor of conjunctiva, tongue, palm or nail beds was moderately sensitive for moderate anemia and very sensitive for severe anemia.
Laboratory patterns for different types of anemia are listed in .

Ferritin is the most accurate diagnostic test for IDA in the elderly and in patients with cirrhosis. A ferritin less than 15 to 19 ng/dL is diagnostic for IDA in the elderly; a higher cutoff is recommended in patients with cirrhosis. Iron deficiency is very unlikely when ferritin is >100 ng/dL. There are different cut off levels of ferritin in the literature. A higher cut-point of ferritin is recommended in diseases of inflammation such as heart failure or chronic kidney disease.

At a threshold of 30 micrograms/L, ferritin is reasonably sensitive with high specificity for iron deficient anemia in people presenting for medical care. The cut off point for ferritin differs with age and individuals with infection or inflammatory disease.
Transferrin saturation may be helpful if a false negative serum ferritin is suspected.

British Society of Gastroenterology guidelines (2021) recommend screening for celiac disease, and upper and lower GI tract endoscopy for persons with confirmed IDA. Fecal immunochemical testing may have a role in risk stratification. Patients with negative upper and lower endoscopy should have capsule endoscopy to evaluate the small bowel as a source of bleeding.
Hemoglobin <11 g/dL is specific but not sensitive for IDA in infants.

If a clear cause for iron deficiency is not found, consider endoscopic evaluation. The risk of colorectal cancer in men age 18 to 49 was 0.78% over 5 years following the diagnosis, versus 0.05% in those without IDA.
See algorithm in for a suggested approach to evaluation.

BSG guidelines (2021) recommend a single dose of ferrous sulfate (elemental iron 65 mg) or ferrous gluconate daily. Higher or more frequent doses cause more side effects without additional benefit.B The usual dose in infants and young children is 3 to 6 mg/kg of elemental iron per day.
Treatment of iron deficiency once per day is as efficacious as a thrice per day regimen.B

Recommended treatment for most patients with IDA is oral iron therapy with the equivalent of 65 mg elemental iron daily using any version of iron supplement (). Higher doses are not necessary and increase side effects.
The usual duration of oral iron is 4 months. Response to therapy should be assessed after 2 to 4 weeks.
A Cochrane review has shown that intermittent iron supplementation may be as effective as daily supplementation in preventing or controlling anemia in adolescents and menstruating adult women.

Oral iron therapy should be taken in a fasting state with no food intake for at least one hour afterward. Taking vitamin C with oral iron is not beneficial. However, dietary increaes in vitamin C to improve absorption of dietary iron sources was found to be beneficial.
Side effects of iron therapy include constipation, diarrhea, nausea, or reflux and are seen in 20% of patients.

Oral iron therapy should be taken on an empty stomach when there is an acidic or neutral environment. Gradually increasing the dose is thought to decrease the risk of adverse effects. Ascorbic acid theoretically potentiates oral iron absorption but taking Vitamin C with iron supplementation did not improve hemoglobin levels after 3 months in one RCT. Avoid antacids and proton pump inhibitors concurrently with iron therapy.
In a meta-analysis of 8 Asian RCTs, H. pylori eradication combined with iron improved IDA more than iron administration alone.

A study of women who had fatigue, ferritin <50 mcg/L and hemoglobin >12.0 g/dl randomized them to FeSO4 or placebo for 12 weeks. Fatigue decreased more in the treated group (48% vs 29%, p = 0.02) on a validated scale.
Low dose ferrous sulfate in children 9 to 48 months of age results in higher hemoglobin and ferritin levels than treatment with iron polysaccharides complex. Both are similarly well tolerated.

For hospitalized patients with anemia and coronary heart disease ACP recommends a restrictive transfusion strategy with a hemoglobin target of 7 to 8. Additionally, erythropoietin should be avoided in CHF patients with mild to moderate anemia. Intravenous iron in patients with heart disease does not improve mortality according to one systematic review of limited data.

Intravenous iron may improve quality of life and decrease hospitalizations in patients with heart failure and iron deficiency anemia. Meta-analyses of intravenous iron therapy in heart failure patients with low reduced left ventricular ejection fraction and iron deficiency (most commonly defined as serum ferritin <100 μg/L or TSAT <20% with ferritin 100–300 μg/L) demonstrated significant reductions in cardiovascular death and heart failure hospitalizations, with greater benefits observed in those with lower baseline iron levels.
An RCT found no improved cardiovascular benefits from titrated amounts of intravenous ferric carboxymaltose compared to placebo for adults with heart failure and iron deficiency.

An ultra-short treatment of intravenous iron, subcutaneous erythropoietin, vitamin B12 and oral folic acid reduced total blood transfusion in patients with preoperative anemia undergoing elective cardiac surgery.

Parenteral iron therapy (iron dextran, iron sucrose, and iron ferric gluconate) is prescribed to patients who cannot tolerate oral iron, have intestinal malabsorption, or are in acute need of iron after erythropoetin or chronic blood loss.
Parenteral iron can be given as a weekly 100 mg dose of elemental iron for patients receiving erythropoietin.

The total dose of parenteral iron is calculated using the following formula: deficit = [Body weight (kg) x 2.4 x (Target hgb − Initial hgb [g/dl])] + 500 mg. So, a 65-kg person with an initial hemoglobin of 8 g/dL and a target of 11 g/dL would have a total dose of [65 x 2.4 x (11 − 8)] + 500 = 968 mg. See manufacturer's instructions for dose and frequency instructions.
A home-based child development program improved cognitive and social-emotional scores in infants (6-12 months of age) with IDA although not as much infants without IDA.

In a meta-analysis of 9 RCTs on the use of IV iron in obstetric and gynecologic patients with iron deficiency anemia, ferric carboxymaltose had better efficacy in increasing hemoglobin and ferritin with fewer side effects as compared to iron sucrose.

Some guidelines consider IV iron supplementation to women with IDA after 34 weeks of gestation. Recent UK guidelines by the British Society for Hematology provide consideration for IV iron supplementation in women who present after 34 weeks of gestation with confirmed iron deficiency anemia and Hb of <100 g/l (1C). The NATA (Network for the advancement of Patient Blood Management, Hemostasis and Thrombosis) consensus statement recommends administration of IV iron in women newl y diagnosed with IDA beyond 34 weeks of gestaion (1B).
Duration of treatment is 4 to 12 months until iron stores are replenished., or three months after stabilization of the hemoglobin
Patients showing signs of decompensation require blood transfusion and consideration for hospitalization.
Side effects of parenteral iron include arthralgias, skin rash, and low-grade fever. These reactions do not preclude treatment.

The most severe reaction that occurs with parenteral iron dextran is anaphylaxis in 0.7% patients, so always give a patient a test dose of 0.25 mg IV iron dextran before administering the complete dosage.

In a systematic literature review, hypophosphatemia associated with intravenous iron is variable, ranging from 0.0% to 92.1% for ferric carboxymaltose and 0.0% to 40.0% for iron sucrose. Most RCTs reported asymptomatic hypophosphatemia. In 11 case reports, severe hypophosphatemia was associated severe fatigue.
There is insufficient evidence that iron therapy improves the psychomotor and cognitive development of iron-deficient children in the age group less than 3 years.C
Treatment of mild anemia in severe CHF improves clinical outcome.C
IDA, when left untreated, proceeds to complete presentation of decompensation and under extreme circumstances to hemoglobin <4 g/dL, which can precipitate heart failure and ensuing death.
IDA, when treated, has a good prognosis, and patients generally return to baseline in 2 months.
Treatment of mild anemia in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction improves clinical outcomes.

There is no convincing evidence that iron therapy improves the psychomotor and cognitive development of iron-deficient children in the age group less than 3 years.Similarly, universal iron supplementation to young children in low-middle income country where anemia is prevalent did not show any benefit on cognitive development.
Hemoglobin increases on iron therapy at 1 gm/dL every 2 to 3 weeks, so it should be checked at 1-month intervals.
It takes 4 to 6 months for iron stores to be replenished.
Vegetarian patients should consume about 20 mg of iron every day via their diet.

In pregnant women with anemia, daily oral iron treatment improves hematological indices but has no clear effect on maternal or fetal outcomes, based on a systematic review of 20 studies. It also causes frequent gastrointestinal adverse effects and has unclear benefits for mothers and babies.

Many organizations recommend to screen for anemia at the first prenatal visit. In an update to its recommendation in 2024, the USPSTF concludes that due to insufficient evidence, the benefits and harms of screening for and supplementing iron in asymptomatic pregnant individuals remain uncertain, and therefore, routine screening and supplementation cannot be recommended..

In non-anemic patients, start low-dose (30 mg elemental iron) supplements at the first prenatal visit. In anemic patients, begin oral iron, 60 to 120 mg (elemental iron) daily. When anemia is corrected, decrease iron to 30 mg/day

If there is no response to iron treatment after 4 weeks of treatment, evaluate compliance and consider further evaluation of anemia. In women of African, Mediterranean, or Southeast Asian ancestry, mild anemia unresponsive to iron therapy may be due to thalassemia minor or sickle cell trait.
A single dose of IV iron compared to oral iron replacement may decrease the rate of low birth weight.

A study of 278 Australian women with iron deficiency compared 500 mg with 1000 mg of IV ferric carboxymaltose in the 2nd or 3rd trimester. Women receiving the lower dose were more likely to require additional IV iron.

Postpartum: A systematic review found several studies comparing erythropoietin with iron supplementation for post-partum anemia. There were no clear benefits of erythropoietin over iron, it is much more costly, and given the concerns over adverse effects particularly in a hypercoagulable state, it cannot be routinely recommended for this indication.Current guidelines for postpartum anemia management recommend that IV iron be considered only after a failed trial of oral iron (secondary to an inadequate hemoglobin response or patient intolerance to oral iron).
See Diagnostic Criteria section for age-specific cutoffs for diagnosis.
Children may present with pallor, fatigue, irritability, and history of pica.
Mild anemia should be treated with 3 mg/kg/day oral iron therapy. For severe anemia, give 6 mg/kg/day oral iron therapy.
Iron therapy does not increase the risk of malaria when regular prevention or management services for malaria are provided.

For children with non-anemic iron deficiency (serum ferritin < 14 mcg/L and hemoglobin >= 110 g/L), adding ferrous sulfate to diet education increased subsequent ferritin levels over diet education alone. There was no measuarable impact on a cognitive score, though.

A randomized trial identified 3300 eight-month-old infants living in Bangladesh who were developmentally normal, living in an area with little iron in the ground water, and did not have severe anemia (hemoglobin < 8 g/dL) or severe malnutrition. The infants were randomized to receive either (1) 12.5 mg elemental iron in a syrup given once daily, plus placebo packets of micronutrient powers; (2) placebo syrup and a micronutrient powder that contained 12.5 mg elemental iron, vitamin A, vitamin C, folic acid, and zinc; or (3) placebo syrup and placebo power. Both immediately after the intervention and 9 months later, there were no differences among either treatment group and placebo with regard to any cognitive or developmental outcomes.
